articles.title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.

articles.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

articles.title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

articles.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

articles.title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.

articles.title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

articles.title: A Rank-One Bypass of Fixed Linear Erasure
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear concept erasure can make a target unreadable to a specified family of linear classifiers applied to a model's current internal features. In an open-weight release, however, an attacker can modify the layers that produce those features. We study a fixed affine erasure layer whose upstream model is allowed to change. If the layer transmits even one direction visible to an allowed downstream classifier, the attacker can write a target score into that direction and carry it through the layer. We show that this condition is also necessary, and that for a nonconstant linear target score the required change is a rank-one affine update. Across six CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks, the route restores nearly all pre-erasure target performance and can leave a deployed benign linear head's scores unchanged to numerical tolerance. We then price the attack: with eight target labels and 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples, a 10% mean relative feature edit yields 79.8% test accuracy, which is 91.2% of the fitted score's gain over chance; tighter edit limits sharply reduce success. Linear guardedness therefore remains a valid guarantee about the current representation, but it is not by itself a tamper-resistance guarantee for an editable open-weight model.

articles.title: PGU-Decoder: Prior-Guided Unified Decoding for Industrial Road-Network Map Updating
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Timely road-network map updates are essential to navigation and autonomous driving. Three key tasks are intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, covering topology, geometry, and attributes, respectively. Separate pipelines duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification, increasing operational costs. We propose PGU-Decoder, a production-grade unified decoding framework for semantic prediction across these tasks. A Prior Query Module (PQM) constructs point-level prior queries from sampled locations on road-network geometries. Fixed reference points preserve positional priors throughout decoding, allowing the model to focus on surrounding context. Point-level representations are aggregated into instance-level representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) captures inter-instance dependencies. Task-specific heads then generate predictions. We validate PGU-Decoder in large-scale automated road-network map updating across more than 360 cities in China, where it consistently outperforms seven baselines. Following deployment at AutoNavi Map, it achieves quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective industrial solution for road-network map updating.

articles.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.23977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. articles.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.

articles.title: Faster to the Wrong Answer: The Price of Local Updates in Federated Optimization
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local computation can improve the conditioning of federated updates but may also introduce bias, causing their fixed point to differ from the global minimizer. We characterize the minimum worst-case bias achievable under a prescribed conditioning bound. We consider strongly convex quadratic client objectives with Hessian eigenvalues in $[\mu,L]$ and local updates represented by a shared positive spectral filter. Client heterogeneity is measured by the root-mean-square gradient at the global minimizer. For a uniform surrogate condition number bounded by $\chi\in[1,L/\mu]$, we establish the exact worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity, $(L-\mu\chi)/(2\mu L\sqrt{\chi})$, and show that local gradient descent with sufficiently small step sizes and proximal updates attain this bound. Our analysis reduces populations of arbitrary dimension, including noncommuting Hessians, to distributions over scalar curvatures. This reduction provides optimality certificates and worst-case constructions involving at most three scalar clients. We further extend the sharp proximal bias bound to smooth strongly convex objectives beyond quadratics and quantify the error introduced by inexact local solves.

articles.title: FDM+: A Framework for Constrained Control of the 2D Radiative Transport Equation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applying the frozen diffusion model (FDM) [29] to the constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation presents several challenges. These include the dimensional difference between control variables and state functions, the resolution mismatch between traditional numerical solvers and deep learning models, and solution non-uniqueness. To address these obstacles, we propose a novel approach, FDM+, which includes three key improvements. Firstly, a decoupled prediction architecture is introduced to address the dimensional heterogeneity. Secondly, an efficient parameterization strategy resolves the resolution mismatch. Meanwhile, we derive a total error bound to analyze how the parameterization error and the model estimation error jointly affect the performance. Thirdly, the conditional distribution learned by the diffusion model is leveraged to perform design space exploration for multi-solution problems. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.

articles.title: VESPA: Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make existing unsafe policies safe, or at least make considerable progress towards safety. Targeted fine-tuning of the existing policy on those counterexamples enables it to learn how to avoid violating safety constraints. We thus use the result of a formal verification as a training signal for fine-tuning. On CartPole, VESPA raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching after two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches after ten. On MountainCarContinuous, VESPA turns an unsafe policy into a safe policy in 53 of 60 runs. We conclude that counterexamples from a verifier are an effective training signal, which can be utilized to systematically improve the safety of policies. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/VESPA-Submission/

articles.title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.

articles.title: QuantAtlas-OM: Taming Neural Spectral Bias in Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Ocean Dynamics
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive neural networks exhibit spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction. As rollouts progress, high-frequency details decay, blurring the predicted fields and destabilizing long-range forecasts. Ocean dynamics offer a particularly stringent test because kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts spanning tens of kilometers. This degradation stems from coupling large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention in a shared feature space. Evolution on a coarse grid smooths out high-wavenumber eddies, whereas evolution on a fine grid amplifies small-scale phase errors and triggers rollout instability. We introduce QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a scale-spectral decoupling framework that confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder. Across physical regimes, the evolution core pairs non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating. Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains $43.7\%$ to $86.5\%$ of mesoscale spectral energy along the $k^{-3}$ cascade at Day $120$, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of $0.81$ to $0.88$ at Day $60$, and reaches $0.66$ at Day $120$ in the Kuroshio ($2.5\times$ to $7.7\times$ the best baselines). articles.title: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Highly parameterized convolutional neural networks often achieve strong predictive performance, but their memory, computation, and deployment costs motivate the search for methods that recover compact architectures from large reference models. We propose SoU-RHS, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with the so-called Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (SoU-SGL). The resulting model sharpens the separation between active and inactive filters, providing an effective mechanism for architecture recovery. A key property of SoU-RHS is stability: across different overparameterized starting widths and under a reasonable range of pruning thresholds, it recovers compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation. This supports the interpretation that the procedure is identifying a compact structure adapted to the data, rather than merely compressing each initial model separately. Across standard image-classification benchmarks, SoU-RHS recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines, while maintaining competitive accuracy, achieving lower negative log-likelihood in every evaluated configuration and generally lower expected calibration error.

articles.title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

articles.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

articles.title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $\Theta(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $\alpha d$ coordinates, $0 < \alpha < 1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $\Theta(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leq\alpha d$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0 < \alpha < 2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

articles.title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.

articles.title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

articles.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Input convex neural networks provide a natural way to enforce convexity globally through architectural constraints. We study how this structure-preserving approximation framework extends to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. For $C^{1,1}$ convex functions on compact convex domains, we establish the sharp $W^{1,p}$ minimax rate $m^{-1/d}$ under max-affine approximation with $m$ affine pieces, and show that every max-affine function admits an exact bounded-width ICNN representation with complexity linear in $m$. The same $W^{1,p}$ approximation rate extends to semiconvex functions through quadratic lifting and to convex transformable functions through monotone composition. For general Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, we develop a quantitative finite-probe approximation theory based on monotone responses to affine projections and obtain a structure-preserving IqCNN with an $L^\infty$ approximation guarantee. We further show that these approximation results extend to ReLU-transferable smooth activations, including Softplus and ELU. Numerical experiments on PDE-based approximation problems compare the proposed architectures with parameter-matched MLPs and validation-tuned shape penalties, demonstrating global structural validity without penalty tuning while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy. Overall, the results identify recoverable convex latent structure as the key mechanism enabling gradient-level structure-preserving approximation beyond convexity.

articles.title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days null. Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, yet the day-to-day variance of the fraction of cells covered is roughly 3 to 10 times what independent cells would give, and misses cluster in time; both effects grow with lead time for the CNN, also appear for HRES, and are shared by all methods. An oracle that divides each day's normalised errors by that day's mean removes 81 to 92 percent of the excess dispersion for the CNN and 93 to 98 percent for HRES, so days of large errors across much of the grid account for most of it. articles.title: OpenGNS: An Open Dataset of the Gradient Noise Scale across Vision, Language, and Diffusion Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/olympique-marcel/OpenGNS

articles.title: Tell Me How Sure You Are: Communicating Uncertainty in Auxiliary Evidence to Foundation Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many queries, the context information provided to generative foundation models, such as LLMs and VLMs, is inherently uncertain, including its representations of the physical world. While conventional prompting discards the associated uncertainty, this paper, for the first time in the literature, systematically demonstrates that communicating such uncertainty in context provides useful additional cues for downstream decisions and yields improvements across a wide range of settings. We formulate the decision-making problem as a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task supported by auxiliary text-based characteristics. We choose this due to the availability of well-defined auxiliary properties, associated uncertainty, and unambiguous task correctness. Using five downstream foundation models across three datasets, we extensively evaluate uncertainty arising from both humans and learned models when observing or predicting auxiliary evidence. Across all settings, we find that communicating uncertainty substantially improves downstream LLM classification performance: macro-F1 improves up to $26.18$ percentage points compared to when the uncertainty information is not communicated. We further observe how the foundation models process such uncertainty information and find that auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive information about the correctness of downstream decisions. Together, these results establish uncertainty as useful contextual information and motivate more systematic consideration of uncertainty communication in future foundation-model inference pipelines.

articles.title: VAFL: A Vertical Analytic Federated Learning Mechanism for Efficient Crowdsourced Services via Closed-Form Solutions
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent services often rely on complementary information held by different organizations, motivating Vertical Federated Learning without centralized raw-data pooling. We propose VAFL, a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning framework that fits classification and regression heads on fixed local representations through regularized least squares. An agent-assisted protected-computation workflow supports two-party and multi-party collaboration. To reduce fitting overhead, we develop a full-dimensional equivalent solve that applies block factors directly to the target matrix, avoiding construction of the full inverse. We further study two width-reduction strategies: local spectral projection with coefficient lifting, and full-dimensional local fitting with low-rank cross-party correction. The first compresses the prediction space, whereas the second retains local components outside the collaboration subspace. We establish their algebraic properties and analyze their computational scope. Experiments on five benchmarks show the accuracy--cost tradeoffs of these strategies and compatibility with diverse frozen backbones. Predictive performance and training time identify useful operating points and the limits of compression.

articles.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $\mu$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $\mu$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $\mu$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGP

articles.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

articles.title: Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

articles.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

articles.title: DyNA-Mixer: Decoupling Time and Topology for Scalable Dynamic Node Affinity Prediction
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-time dynamic graphs preserve the ordering, timing, and evolving strength of interactions that static snapshots discard, making dynamic graph mining essential for evolving systems such as recommender systems, trade networks, and transaction platforms. Research in this area has centered on dynamic link prediction, which forecasts only whether a future interaction will occur, whereas many applications also need its intensity. The dynamic node affinity prediction (DNAP) problem generalizes this task to continuous targets and full-candidate ranking, making it more broadly applicable but substantially harder. This raises two coupled difficulties: ranking requires a predictor expressive enough to capture both multi-scale temporal evolution and graph-wide collaborative patterns, yet running such a predictor over every source--destination pair is computationally prohibitive. We propose DyNA-Mixer, which decouples temporal forecasting from collaborative structure modeling. It adopts a multi-scale temporal predictor for pair-specific affinity evolution, constructs a Virtual Collaborative Graph that infers query-time relationships and aggregates trends from related interactions, and fuses the two through a gated residual mechanism. A sparsity-aware evaluation strategy further restricts expensive forecasting to pairs with recent non-zero affinities. Experiments on four Temporal Graph Benchmark datasets for the DNAP problem show that DyNA-Mixer achieves new state-of-the-art NDCG@10 on every dataset, including a 17.8\% relative test improvement over the strongest baseline on tgbn-token, the largest dataset.

articles.title: ICICLE: In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization allocates training budget by predicting how partially observed learning curves will continue. LC-PFN first applied prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) to learning-curve extrapolation, and FT-PFN extended this approach to configuration-aware freeze-thaw optimization with a ten-slot hyperparameter encoder. We introduce In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation (ICICLE), an in-context surrogate that accepts a variable number of hyperparameters through a shared set encoder and is trained on a synthetic prior covering typed hyperparameters, heavy-tailed noise, quantization, and divergence. ICICLE has 1.28 million parameters (8.7% of FT-PFN's count) and produces similar mean-regret trajectories to FT-PFN on LCBench, PD1, and TaskSet. On the 86-task Meta-Album benchmark with 33 hyperparameters, ICICLE reaches lower mean normalized regret than Quick-Tune overall and on extended, with no clear difference on mini or micro. It does so without pre-training or meta-training on Meta-Album tasks, whereas Quick-Tune is meta-trained on related Meta-Album tasks. Our release samples synthetic training tasks on the fly and provides a freeze-thaw scheduler for Ray Tune and an ONNX model for inference without JAX or PyTorch.

articles.title: Latent Action Policies from Suboptimal Data
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.

articles.title: The geometry of neural network decision boundaries
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are built using well-understood mathematical operations, yet their complex nature poses significant challenges to intuitively understanding their decision-making processes. This work introduces a method for visualizing and measuring ANN decision boundary geometry directly in the high-dimensional input space, avoiding distortions found with traditional projection-based techniques. We analyze boundary curvatures and distances in diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods. Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as the size of the subspace increases, suggesting that decision boundaries are close to input samples within large, continuous subspaces. We also quantify how much boundary distances and curvatures reduce near dataset samples after adversarial training. Training methodology has a significantly stronger impact on boundary distance and curvature than architecture or test-set accuracy. These findings are contextualized within prior work, supporting or refuting several previously proposed theories of boundary behavior. Our analytically and empirically supported methodology lays the foundation for future studies to improve network interpretability and understanding.

articles.title: From Activity Recognition to Shift Detection: Variational Wi-Fi Sensing with Evidential Uncertainty
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human motion perturbs wireless channels, making commodity Wi-Fi devices a practical platform for device-free activity recognition. Yet Channel State Information (CSI) also depends strongly on the person, receiver position, recording session, and surrounding environment, so a classifier can continue producing activity labels after its deployment conditions have moved away from those seen during training. We propose Wi-HAR, a multi-antenna architecture in which four Variational Auto-Encoders learn compact distributions from raw Wi-Fi 6 CSI magnitudes and a delayed-fusion classifier combines their means and log-variances. On twelve activities from a public benchmark, Wi-HAR reaches 96.6% median recognition accuracy, compared with 70.8-81.5% for independently optimized single-antenna models, showing that the antennas provide complementary views of the same activity. We then use the same latent backbone to detect deployment shifts without using shifted samples for model selection or calibration. A class-conditional uncertainty score derived from Evidential Deep Learning achieves a macro-average ROC-AUC of 0.897 across eleven datasets that change receiver position, participant, recording session, or room, and detects 82.5% of shifted samples at a realized 5.2% in-distribution rejection rate. Detection performance nevertheless varies substantially across receiver positions, showing that the same physical change does not induce a uniform uncertainty response. The compact representation also supports shallow decision-tree analysis using variables from several antennas.

articles.title: Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA) for Plant Spectroscopy
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. articles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.

articles.title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24626v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

articles.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.

articles.title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $\sigma^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically

articles.title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

articles.title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.

articles.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

articles.title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $\mu$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

articles.title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

articles.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming with Basis Function Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a novel approach for approximating the value function in Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our approach is grounded in the approximate linear programming (ALP) framework, wherein basis functions (BFs) play an important role. Traditionally, BFs have been pre-defined, randomly generated, or restricted to specific structures, which both limits the accuracy that can be achieved and leaves no mechanism for improving a given approximation. We instead learn BFs from the model itself, by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. We introduce the Bellman operator basis function (BOBF) learning method, and prove that each learned BF improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function. Its shrunken counterpart (SBOBF) retains this guarantee while capping the number of BFs, and therefore the computational effort per iteration. For large-scale problems, where the number of constraints is prohibitive, we develop hybrid variants (HBOBF and SHBOBF) that combine constraint sampling with BF learning, and we show that the improvement and finite-termination guarantees are preserved under explicitly stated conditions. Numerical experiments on (continuous) perishable inventory and queueing control problems demonstrate that our BF learning techniques significantly outperform existing methods in the literature.

articles.title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.

articles.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. articles.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schr\"odinger Bridges
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schr\"odinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schr\"odinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

articles.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.24764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.
